claim: Cranial kinesis is found in living vertebrates only in some squamates and crown birds.
source: The independent movements and flexibility of various parts of the skull, called cranial kinesis, are an evolutionary innovation that is found in living vertebrates only in some squamates and crown birds
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: Cranial kinesis is considered to be a major factor underpinning much of the enormous phenotypic and ecological diversity of living birds.
source: cranial kinesis, are an evolutionary innovation that is found in living vertebrates only in some squamates and crown birds and is considered to be a major factor underpinning much of the enormous phenotypic and ecological diversity of living birds, the most diverse group of extant amniotes
evidence: This represents a widely accepted hypothesis in the field, referenced as established knowledge.

claim: Birds are the most diverse group of extant amniotes.
source: living birds, the most diverse group of extant amniotes
evidence: This is stated as a fact based on established taxonomic knowledge.

claim: Understanding of the evolutionary assemblage of the characteristic modern bird skull has been hampered by sparse fossil records of early cranial materials.
source: Compared to the postcranium, our understanding of the evolutionary assemblage of the characteristic modern bird skull has been hampered by sparse fossil records of early cranial materials
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about the state of the field.

claim: Yuanchuavis kompsosoura is an Early Cretaceous enantiornithine bird.
source: the Early Cretaceous enantiornithine Yuanchuavis kompsosoura
evidence: This is a taxonomic and temporal assignment based on prior description and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The skull of Yuanchuavis kompsosoura shows evolutionary and functional conservation of the temporal and palatal regions by retaining the ancestral theropod dinosaurian configuration.
source: Our reconstruction of the skull shows evolutionary and functional conservation of the temporal and palatal regions by retaining the ancestral theropod dinosaurian configuration within the skull of this otherwise derived and volant bird.
evidence: This is supported by detailed anatomical descriptions and comparisons presented in the Results section.

claim: Loss of the jugal process of the palatine represents the first step in the structural modifications of this element leading to the kinetic crown bird condition.
source: Geometric morphometric analysis of the palatine suggests that loss of the jugal process represents the first step in the structural modifications of this element leading to the kinetic crown bird condition.
evidence: This is based on geometric morphometric analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Yuanchuavis manifests the key role of evolutionary mosaicism and experimentation in early bird diversification.
source: The mixture of plesiomorphic temporal and palatal structures together with a derived avialan rostrum and postcranial skeleton encapsulated in Yuanchuavis manifests the key role of evolutionary mosaicism and experimentation in early bird diversification.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the combination of features observed in the specimen.

claim: Many evolutionary novelties associated with living birds originated among early lineages.
source: The growing fossil record of Mesozoic avialans has revealed that the initial appearance of many evolutionary novelties associated with living birds in fact originated among early lineages (Xu et al., 2014; Brusatte et al., 2015; Chiappe and Meng, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Much research interest in early bird evolution has focused on flight-relevant morphologies.
source: Much of the research interest in the early evolution of birds has focused on flight-relevant morphologies (Sullivan et al., 2017; Heers et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a characterization of the field supported by citations.

claim: Little is known about how the bulky and akinetic dinosaurian skull became transformed into the delicate, kinetic, and functionally diverse extant bird skull.
source: However, little is known about how the bulky and akinetic dinosaurian skull became transformed into the delicate, kinetic, and functionally diverse extant bird skull (Bhullar et al., 2016)
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: The kinetic skull is inferred to have contributed significantly to the spectacular adaptive radiation of birds, culminating in >10,000 species recognized today.
source: which is inferred to have contributed significantly to their spectacular adaptive radiation, culminating in >10,000 species recognized today (Zusi, 1984; Bout and Zweers, 2001; Gill, 2007; Bhullar et al., 2016; Olsen and Gremillet, 2017)
evidence: This is an inference supported by multiple citations.

claim: The lack of resolution about cranial evolution results in part from the rarity of cranial materials of early avialans and limited data from conventional examination methods.
source: This lack of resolution results in part from the rarity of cranial materials of early avialans and the limited data available from conventional methods of examination given their typically poor and two-dimensional preservation (Witmer and Martin, 1987; O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a).
evidence: This is an explanation supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Some previous studies have overstated the cranial resemblance between stem and crown birds, including positing the existence of certain bony contacts and intracranial joints required for kinesis not yet confirmed in fossil taxa.
source: Meanwhile, some previous studies have perhaps overstated the cranial resemblance between stem and crown birds, including positing the existence of certain bony contacts and intracranial joints (e.g. pterygoid-quadrate joint) required for kinesis, though yet to be confirmed positively in fossil taxa (Witmer and Martin, 1987; Holliday and Witmer, 2008; Wang et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: Yuanchuavis kompsosoura is phylogenetically assigned to the second earliest branching enantiornithine clade (Pengornithidae).
source: Yuanchuavis phylogenetically is assigned to the second earliest branching enantiornithine clade (Pengornithidae)
evidence: This is a phylogenetic placement based on previous analysis.

claim: Yuanchuavis kompsosoura preserves a unique pintail feather morphotype that has been inferred to be used for sexual display.
source: and preserves a unique pintail feather morphotype that has been inferred to be used for sexual display (Wang et al., 2021b)
evidence: This is based on a previous description and functional inference.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the premaxillae are unfused.
source: Like in other pengornithids (Zhou et al., 2008; Hu et al., 2015; O'Connor et al., 2016a), the premaxillae are unfused.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen, compared with other taxa.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the short premaxillary corpus is rostrocaudally longer than dorsoventrally high, with subparallel dorsal and ventral margins.
source: As in most Early Cretaceous enantiornithines including other pengornithids except for Chiappeavis (Zhou et al., 2008; Hu et al., 2015; O'Connor et al., 2016a), the short premaxillary corpus is rostrocaudally longer than dorsoventrally high, with subparallel dorsal and ventral margins (Figures 1 and 2a; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen and figures, compared with other taxa.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the maxillary process of the premaxilla extends beyond the rostrocaudal midpoint of the external naris.
source: The maxillary process of the premaxilla extends beyond the rostrocaudal midpoint of the external naris, which is proportionately longer than the state in other pengornithids where it terminates caudally within the rostral fourth of the external naris (Zhou et al., 2008; Hu et al., 2015; O'Connor et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen, compared with other taxa.

claim: Yuanchuavis has six premaxillary teeth on each side.
source: Six premaxillary teeth are present on each side (Figure 2b), not five as estimated in a previous study (Wang et al., 2021b)
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen and figure, correcting a previous count.

claim: Six premaxillary teeth in Yuanchuavis is greater than the maximum number of four in other avialans.
source: and this is greater than the maximum number of four in other avialans (Louchart and Viriot, 2011; O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a; Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the tooth crowns are weakly expanded, and the tapered apices are slightly recurved.
source: As in other pengornithids (Zhou et al., 2008; Hu et al., 2015; O'Connor et al., 2016a), the tooth crowns are weakly expanded, and the tapered apices are slightly recurved.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen, compared with other taxa.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the triradiate maxilla constitutes the major portion of the facial margin.
source: The triradiate maxilla constitutes the major portion of the facial margin as in other early avialans (Figure 2c; O'Connor et al., 2011b; Wang et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen and figure, compared with other taxa.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the ascending process of the maxilla lacks the fenestra present in Pengornis.
source: The ascending process lacks the fenestra present in Pengornis (Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen, compared with another taxon.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the broad jugal process of the maxilla is sharply constricted along its caudal fourth, a unique feature otherwise unknown among early-diverging avialans.
source: The broad jugal process is sharply constricted along its caudal fourth, a unique feature otherwise unknown among early-diverging avialans (O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a; Rauhut et al., 2018; Kundrát et al., 2019; O'Connor et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021a)
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen, compared with other taxa via citations.

claim: Yuanchuavis has nine maxillary teeth.
source: Nine maxillary teeth are present (seven preserved teeth and two additional alveoli preserved in the right maxilla)
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen.

claim: Nine maxillary teeth in Yuanchuavis exceeds the number present in some enantiornithines (e.g. bohaiornithids).
source: which like in other pengornithids exceeds the number present in some enantiornithines (e.g. bohaiornithids; O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the nasal is weakly bowed ventrally and tapered at both ends.
source: The nasal is weakly bowed ventrally and tapered at both ends (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen and figure.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, a maxillary process of the nasal is absent.
source: A maxillary process, present in Parapengornis and other enantiornithines (Zhou et al., 2005; O'Connor et al., 2011b; Wang et al., 2021b), is absent.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen, compared with other taxa.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the elongate nasals contact medially for almost their entire length such that the premaxillae and frontals do not contact.
source: The elongate nasals contact medially for almost their entire length such that the premaxillae and frontals do not contact.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the rostral end of the nasal is forked as in Pengornis.
source: The rostral end of the nasal is forked as in Pengornis (Zhou et al., 2008) and receives the caudal tapered portion of the nasal process of the premaxilla (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen and figure, compared with another taxon.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the nasal has a width-to-length ratio of 0.11, notably more slender than in some enantiornithines but wider than in Falcatakely.
source: The nasal has a width-to-length ratio of 0.11, notably more slender than in some enantiornithines (e.g. Eoenantiornis and Protopteryx) but wider than in Falcatakely (O'Connor et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a measurement from the specimen, compared with other taxa.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the nasal is not perforated by a foramen, in contrast to Pengornis.
source: In contrast to Pengornis (Zhou et al., 2008), the bone is not perforated by a foramen.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen, compared with another taxon.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the lacrimal is triradiate with a robust descending ramus that is longer and wider than the more delicate rostral ramus, which in turn is twice the length of the caudal ramus.
source: The lacrimal is triradiate with a robust descending ramus that is longer and wider than the more delicate rostral ramus, which in turn is twice the length of the caudal ramus (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen and figure.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the straight dorsal margin of the lacrimal lacks the central concavity characteristic of Pengornis.
source: The straight dorsal margin of the lacrimal lacks the central concavity characteristic of Pengornis (Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen, compared with another taxon.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the descending ramus of the lacrimal lacks the ventral expansion seen in Falcatakely and Ichthyornis.
source: The descending ramus widens rostrocaudally along its central portion and then narrows toward the ventral end, lacking the ventral expansion seen in Falcatakely and Ichthyornis (O'Connor et al., 2020; Torres et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen, compared with other taxa.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, an oval fenestra is developed near the caudal margin of the descending ramus of the lacrimal at the dorsoventral midpoint, which is absent in other early avialans including other pengornithids.
source: An oval fenestra is developed near its caudal margin at the dorsoventral midpoint (recognized on both sides), which is absent in other early avialans including other pengornithids (Mayr et al., 2005; O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a; Zhou et al., 2013; O'Connor et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen, compared with other taxa.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the lacrimal bears a triradiate lateral embossment forming crests along each ramus, centered at the juncture of the three rami.
source: The lacrimal bears a triradiate lateral embossment forming crests along each ramus, and it is centered at the juncture of the three rami.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen.

claim: The triradiate lateral embossment on the lacrimal of Yuanchuavis has not been described among other early avialans but is present in deinonychosaurians.
source: No similar structure has yet been described among other early avialans (O'Connor et al., 2011b; Rauhut et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021a), but this morphology is present in deinonychosaurians (Norell et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the preserved left prefrontal is similar to the condition in Archaeopteryx.
source: The preserved left prefrontal is similar to the condition in Archaeopteryx (Rauhut et al., 2018) and consistent with the relatively short proportion of the caudal ramus of the lacrimal (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen and figure, compared with another taxon.

claim: The postorbital is an enigmatic element poorly known among enantiornithines.
source: The postorbital is an enigmatic element poorly known among enantiornithines (likely independently reduced in some taxa; Xu et al., 2021) but is preserved exquisitely here (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the Y-shaped postorbital has a pointed frontal process and a blunter squamosal process that is oriented at a near right angle to one another.
source: The Y-shaped postorbital has a pointed frontal process and a blunter squamosal process that is oriented at a near right angle to one another.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the squamosal process of the postorbital is shorter than the frontal process and ends in a blunt articular surface for the squamosal.
source: The squamosal process is shorter than the frontal process and ends in a blunt articular surface for the squamosal.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the jugal process of the postorbital is approximately four times longer than the frontal process, delicate, and deflected caudoventrally.
source: The jugal process is approximately four times longer than the frontal process, delicate, and deflected caudoventrally.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen.

claim: The squamosal is another poorly known cranial element in enantiornithines that has been recognized in only two specimens.
source: The squamosal is another poorly known cranial element in enantiornithines that has been recognized in only two specimens (LP-4450-IEI and IVPP V12707; O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: The squamosal of Yuanchuavis is morphologically more similar to that of Archaeopteryx and non-avialan theropods such as Deinonychus than to other known enantiornithine squamosals.
source: Compared to those specimens, the squamosal of Yuanchuavis is morphologically more similar to that of Archaeopteryx and non-avialan theropods such as Deinonychus, attesting to its relatively large size, the robust quadratojugal process, and the rostrally deeply forked postorbital process (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is a comparative observation from the specimen and figure.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the postorbital process of the squamosal is not forked, in contrast to LP-4450-IEI and IVPP V12707.
source: In contrast, the postorbital process is not forked in LP-4450-IEI and IVPP V12707 (O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a; Wang et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the notch in the postorbital process of the squamosal is deeper than in Archaeopteryx but not as pronounced as in Deinonychus.
source: The notch in the postorbital process is deeper than in Archaeopteryx (Elżanowski and Wellnhofer, 1996) but not as pronounced as in Deinonychus (Ostrom, 1969).
evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by citations.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the dorsal and ventral branches of the postorbital process of the squamosal are subequal in length, as in Archaeopteryx.
source: As in Archaeopteryx (Elżanowski and Wellnhofer, 1996), the dorsal and ventral branches of the postorbital process are subequal in length; whereas the ventral branch is longer in Deinonychus (Ostrom, 1969).
evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by citations.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the trapezoidal-shaped quadratojugal process of the squamosal bears a pointed rostroventral corner that projects as far rostrally as the postorbital process.
source: The trapezoidal-shaped quadratojugal process bears a pointed rostroventral corner that projects as far rostrally as the postorbital process.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the quadratojugal process of the squamosal is trapezoidal-shaped, in contrast to the slender and rod-like form in Archaeopteryx and other enantiornithines and the triangular form in non-avialan theropods.
source: In contrast, the quadratojugal process is slender and rod-like in Archaeopteryx and other enantiornithines and is triangular in non-avialan theropods (Ostrom, 1969; Norell et al., 2006; O'Connor et al., 2011b; Xu et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the paroccipital process of the squamosal is sharply tapered as it projects caudally, and it is connected with the quadratojugal process by a roughly straight ventral margin, resembling the condition in Linheraptor.
source: The paroccipital process is sharply tapered as it projects caudally, and it is connected with the quadratojugal process by a roughly straight ventral margin, resembling the condition in Linheraptor (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen, compared with another taxon.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the unfused frontals and parietals are crushed, revealing few features except that the skull roof is vaulted dorsally.
source: The unfused frontals and parietals are crushed, revealing few features except that the skull roof is vaulted dorsally.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, there is an elongate ridge along the lateral edge of the frontal forming a concave margin around the dorsal margin of the orbit.
source: There is an elongate ridge along the lateral edge of the frontal forming a concave margin around the dorsal margin of the orbit, and this ridge runs for most of the length of the frontal.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the frontal does not appear to have contributed to a postorbital process.
source: The frontal does not appear to have contributed to a postorbital process.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the quadrate has a bicondylar mandibular process, as in other early avialans and non-avialan theropods.
source: As in other early avialans and non-avialan theropods (Turner et al., 2012; Hendrickx et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2021a), the quadrate has a bicondylar mandibular process (Figure 2h–j, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c-e).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen and figures, compared with other taxa.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the medial condyle of the quadrate is larger than the lateral one, like in some other enantiornithines but not Longipteryx.
source: Like in some other enantiornithines but not Longipteryx (O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a; Stidham and O'Connor, 2021), the medial condyle is larger than the lateral one (Figure 2j).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen and figure, compared with other taxa.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the caudal surface of the quadrate corpus is not perforated by a foramen, as in some enantiornithines including Pengornis and Shenqiornis.
source: The caudal surface of the quadrate corpus is not perforated by a foramen as in some enantiornithines including Pengornis and Shenqiornis (Zhou et al., 2008; O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen, compared with other taxa.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the caudal margin of the quadrate is concave and bowed with the medial and lateral mandibular condyles positioned caudally relative to the corpus, as in the juvenile enantiornithine IVPP V12707.
source: In lateral view, the caudal margin of the quadrate is concave and bowed with the medial and lateral mandibular condyles positioned caudally relative to the corpus as in the juvenile enantiornithine IVPP V12707 (Wang et al., 2021a), rather than being level with the shaft as in non-avialan theropods such as Linheraptor (Turner et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen, compared with other taxa.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the bowing of the quadrate is restricted to the ventral half with the caudal margin being relatively straight in the dorsal half, and the absence of cracks in the corpus supports this as the original morphology.
source: The bowing is restricted to the ventral half of the quadrate with the caudal margin (lateral view) being relatively straight in the dorsal half, and the absence of cracks in the corpus supports this as the original morphology (Figure 2h and j).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen and figure, with inference about preservation.

claim: The morphology of the quadrate in Yuanchuavis suggests that the quadrate was inclined with the otic process positioned caudal to the mandibular process.
source: This morphology also suggests that the quadrate was inclined with the otic process positioned caudal to the mandibular process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed morphology.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, there is a shallow concavity separating the medial and lateral condyles of the quadrate near the mediolateral midpoint of the mandibular process.
source: There is a shallow concavity separating the medial and lateral condyles near the mediolateral midpoint of the mandibular process (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen and figure.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, there does not appear to be a rostral or caudal labrum around the condyles of the quadrate, but the medial condyle faces a bit caudally and is raised up above the adjacent bone surface.
source: There does not appear to be a rostral or caudal labrum around the condyles, but the medial condyle faces a bit caudally and is raised up above the adjacent bone surface (also visible on the left quadrate).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the lateral edge of the mandibular process of the quadrate is broken so that the morphology of the articulation with the quadratojugal cannot be identified in detail, but the remnants are directed and extended somewhat rostrally, similar to the state in Linheraptor.
source: The lateral edge of the mandibular process is broken so that the morphology of the articulation with the quadratojugal cannot be identified in detail, but the remnants are directed and extended somewhat rostrally, in a manner similar to the state present in Linheraptor where it has rostrocaudally elongate contact with the quadratojugal.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen with inference about the original morphology, compared with another taxon.

claim: The rostrocaudally elongate contact between the quadrate and quadratojugal has not been identified in other enantiornithines.
source: That elongation has not been identified in other enantiornithines.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on knowledge of other taxa.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the caudal surface of the quadrate corpus forms a sharp crest along its dorsoventral length from the otic head ventrally to just dorsal to the concavity between the medial and lateral mandibular condyles.
source: The caudal surface of the quadrate corpus forms a sharp crest along its dorsoventral length from the otic head ventrally to just dorsal to the concavity between the medial and lateral mandibular condyles.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen.

claim: The sharp caudal crest on the quadrate is present in many, but not all enantiornithines.
source: That sharp caudal crest is present in many, but not all enantiornithines.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on knowledge of other taxa.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, a distinct pterygoid condyle is absent on the quadrate, like IVPP V12707 and non-avialan theropods.
source: Like IVPP V12707 and non-avialan theropods (Norell et al., 2006; Hendrickx et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2021a), a distinct pterygoid condyle is absent on the quadrate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen and figure, compared with other taxa.

claim: The absence of a distinct pterygoid condyle on the quadrate indicates the absence of a condylar-based joint between the quadrate and pterygoid, a derived feature present in Ichthyornis, hesperornithiforms, and crown taxa.
source: indicating the absence of a condylar-based joint between the quadrate and pterygoid, a derived feature present in Ichthyornis, hesperornithiforms, and crown taxa (Gingerich, 1976; Baumel and Witmer, 1993; Field et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed morphology, with comparative information from citations.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the shape of the orbital process of the quadrate is nearly identical to that of Archaeopteryx and non-avialan theropods in having a rounded and blunt convex rostral apex with a straight dorsal margin that extends to the otic process.
source: The shape of the orbital process is nearly identical to that of Archaeopteryx and non-avialan theropods (called the pterygoid ramus) in having a rounded and blunt convex rostral apex with a straight dorsal margin that extends to the otic process (Figure 2h; Currie, 1995; Norell et al., 2006; Hendrickx et al., 2015; Rauhut et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen and figure, compared with other taxa.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the orbital process of the quadrate is dorsoventrally thick and has a rounded rostral apex, in contrast to the dorsoventrally thin and rostrally tapering form in other enantiornithines.
source: In contrast, the orbital process is dorsoventrally thin and tapers rostrally in other enantiornithines (Sander et al., 2001; Stidham and O'Connor, 2021; Wang et al., 2021a)
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: The orbital process of the quadrate is further modified into a narrower, pointed process in Ichthyornis and more crownward taxa.
source: which is further modified into a narrower, pointed process in Ichthyornis and more crownward taxa (Elżanowski and Stidham, 2011; Field et al., 2018b; Torres et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the apex of the orbital process of the quadrate is in the ventral half of the quadrate like Sapeornis and enantiornithines but differs from the position near the dorsoventral midpoint in many non-avialans, Archaeopteryx, and ornithurines.
source: In addition, its apex is in the ventral half of the quadrate like Sapeornis and enantiornithines but differs from the position near the dorsoventral midpoint in many non-avialans, Archaeopteryx, and ornithurines (Elżanowski and Stidham, 2011; Field et al., 2018b; Stidham and O'Connor, 2021; Wang et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen, compared with other taxa.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the orbital process of the quadrate extends dorsally, and it lowers in height ending ventral to the undivided otic head.
source: The orbital process extends dorsally, and it lowers in height ending ventral to the undivided otic head.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the lateral surface of the orbital process of the quadrate is relatively smooth.
source: The lateral surface of the orbital process is relatively smooth.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the medial side of the orbital process of the quadrate appears a bit rougher, and its dorsal edge thickens rostrally.
source: The medial side appears a bit rougher, and its dorsal edge thickens rostrally (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen and figure.

claim: In Yuanchuavis, the ventral margin of the orbital process of the quadrate thickens ventrally near its base and extends ventrally as an orbitocondylar crest, contacting the area near the dorsal edge of the medial apex of the medial mandibular condyle.
source: The ventral margin of the orbital process thickens ventrally near its base and extends ventrally as an orbitocondylar crest, contacting the area near the dorsal edge of the medial apex of the medial mandibular condyle (Figure 2i, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimen and figures.

claim: The orbitocondylar crest on the quadrate is not yet known among other enantiornithines.
source: The orbitocondylar crest is not yet known among other enantiornithines (Elżanowski and Stidham, 2011; Field et al., 2018b; Wang et al., 2021a).
